BERLIN, July 9.—A new pneumatic telecompass, which is said to enable an airman to keep his course mechanically, will be used for the first time in the history of trans-Atlantic aviation by the three German pilots who are planning to attempt flights to America.


Profiting by the mishaps which occurred to the compasses used by the American trans-ocean fliers, Clarence Chamberlain and Commander Richard Byrd, the German aviators will not employ the induction compasses.


The pneumatic compasses have been constructed by the Askania works of Friedenau, suburb of Berlin. They will be installed in the Caspar biplane, in which Otto Koennecke and Count Solms-Laubach hope to reach the United States, and in the two Junkers 2-33 monoplanes which, it was indicated today, will be piloted by Johann Risticz and Frederick Loose.

It is fitted in the stern of the cockpit, where the effect of magnetic influences is at the minimum. Compensation, therefore, becomes unnecessary.

with cap pulled pretty well over his
face, pointing gun at my brother,
and I heard him say, 'Stick em up.'
I could see that my brother did, but
the young man said again, 'Stick
em up higher.' My brother said,
'All right, all right,'" she testified.
"I kept behind a post, so the
man wouldn't see me, and when my
brother and he disappeared down
the hall and into the back room, I
ran out toward the front door." With a nervous tremble in her
voice, Mrs. Bowen continued to de-
scribe Buchanan's entrance to the
hotel to arrest the youth.


Alger had sought hiding in the
Boyer House, following a gun battle
with police. The college student
was charged with attempting to
steal an auto, which led to his ar-
rest.


"I heard three shots; then some-
one said: 'He's got me,'" said the
witness.
"The State's evidence will take up
Monday and part of Tuesday," it
was said.


Other State's witnesses to be heard
are: Carl Shaffer, alleged to have
been wounded in the youth's fight
by a bullet from Ayer's gun;
Coleman said to have been beaten
by Alger; a Negro tailor in whose
arms Buchanan died; and Mr. and
Mrs. Brizentine, whose car was
commandeered in Ayer's flight.
